paragraphs.heading: A fluid that is also a tissue
paragraphs.text: Blood is a body fluid that delivers what cells need, such as nutrients and oxygen, and carries their metabolic waste away. It counts as a specialized kind of connective tissue, given that it is made of cells and cell fragments floating in a liquid called plasma. The pumping of the heart drives it around the body through the blood vessels.

paragraphs.heading: Plasma
paragraphs.text: Plasma makes up about 55% of blood, and on its own it is straw-yellow. It is mostly water, about 92%, with around 8% proteins and small traces of other materials. It carries hormones and dissolved nutrients, for example glucose, amino acids and fatty acids, and it takes away wastes such as carbon dioxide, urea and lactic acid. An average person has 2.7 to 3.0 liters of plasma.

paragraphs.heading: Red blood cells
paragraphs.text: Red blood cells, also called erythrocytes, are the most common cells in blood. They contain hemoglobin, which binds oxygen in a reversible way and so helps blood carry it. Red cells fill about 45% of the blood's volume, a share known as the hematocrit. In mammals, mature red cells have no nucleus and no organelles. Blood looks bright red when its hemoglobin holds oxygen and dark red when it does not.

paragraphs.heading: White cells and platelets
paragraphs.text: White blood cells, or leukocytes, are part of the immune system. They attack infectious agents and foreign substances, and they destroy and clear away old or abnormal cells and debris; cancer of these cells is called leukemia. Platelets take part in clotting: they form a plug, and fibrin from the clotting process builds a mesh over it. Platelets exist only in mammals, and other vertebrates rely on small spindle cells called thrombocytes to clot their blood instead.

paragraphs.heading: Kept in a narrow range
paragraphs.text: The body keeps blood pH between 7.35 and 7.45, which is slightly basic. Below that range blood is too acidic, above it too basic, and a pH under 6.9 or over 7.8 is usually lethal. Several balancing mechanisms hold pH, oxygen, carbon dioxide and bicarbonate steady, working mainly through the respiratory system and the urinary system. A test called an arterial blood gas measures these values.

paragraphs.heading: The round trip
paragraphs.text: In humans, the strong left ventricle of the heart pushes blood out through arteries to the tissues, and veins bring it back to the right atrium. In animals with lungs, the blood in the arteries carries oxygen from inhaled air to the tissues. The blood in the veins carries carbon dioxide, a waste of cell metabolism, back to the lungs to be breathed out. An average adult has roughly 5 litres of blood, about 7% of body weight, and its density is very close to that of pure water.
